content.text: {"relation":"DIVERGENT","consensus_summary":"All four blind responses converge on the same core: 'the heart of the earth' (Matt 12:40) refers to Jesus' burial in the grave/tomb and, in much traditional interpretation, his sojourn in Sheol/Hades, during the interval between death and resurrection, as the antitype of Jonah in the fish. The Jerusalem/center-of-the-land reading is noted only as a minority or rare alternative (Responses A and C explicitly; B folds it into a minority 'grip of earthly authorities' reading).","book_summary":"The book identifies 'the heart of the earth' as Jerusalem — the navel and heart of the land — citing Ezekiel 5:5 and 38:12 for Jerusalem/Israel as set 'in the midst' of the nations/land. It explicitly flags the grave/Hades reading as merely the 'commonly taught' view, signaling rejection of it as the primary referent.","consensus_core_identification":"The grave/tomb (and by traditional extension Sheol/Hades) where Christ lay between death and resurrection.","book_core_identification":"Jerusalem, the geographic-theological center ('navel/heart') of the land, as the place where the Son of Man would be for three days and nights.","core_relation":"CONTRADICTS","extension_relation":"PARTIAL_RECLASSIFICATION","boundary_disagreement":"Under the consensus reading the 'three days and three nights' begin at burial and denote entombment/the realm of the dead; under the book's reading the referent is a location (Jerusalem/the land's center), which typically shifts the covered period to include Jesus' betrayal, custody, trials, and passion within Jerusalem, not only the time in the tomb. The tomb interval may remain inside the book's extension (the tomb is in/near Jerusalem), but the identifying category is relocated from the underworld/grave to the city/land.","material_contradiction":"The book replaces the central referent: 'heart of the earth' names Jerusalem as center of the land, not the grave or Hades. The consensus core says the phrase denotes Christ's entombment/state of death; the book's common-view note explicitly marks that as merely the taught view it departs from. Both cannot be the primary sense of the same phrase in the same context — one is a subterranean/mortuary referent, the other a geographic one — so accepting the book requires rejecting the consensus identification.","rationale":"The minimum cores materially differ: grave/Sheol versus Jerusalem-as-navel-of-the-land. The book's reading corresponds to what the consensus responses themselves classify as a minority/rare alternative (A's third alternative citing exactly Ezek 5:5 and 38:12), which confirms it is a recognizable but non-consensus position — hence DIVERGENT rather than NOVEL. It is not REFINED because the book does not merely adjust the boundary of the grave/Hades referent; it substitutes a different referent, with the extension only partially overlapping (the entombment happens at Jerusalem, and the counted period is likely reclassified to include pre-burial events).","citation_support":"PARTIAL","strongest_objection":"Matthew 12:40's parallel with Jonah 'in the whale's belly' strongly suggests confinement in death, not residence in a city; Jonah's own prayer locates him 'in the belly of Sheol' (Jonah 2:2), and the Ezekiel texts say Jerusalem is in the midst of the nations/land but never use the phrase 'heart of the earth,' so the identification rests on an inferential bridge rather than direct lexical equivalence. Moreover, Jesus was already in Jerusalem before his arrest, straining the 'three days and nights' as time 'in' Jerusalem.","confidence":"high"}
